content.title: Elections
content.text: Defining ElectionsElections are the primary mechanism through which citizens participate in modern political systems. Most scholars regard them as the cornerstone of democratic regimes, enabling citizens to select political leaders and influence policy direction. In democratic contexts, elections typically meet the criteria of being “free, fair, and competitive,” thereby allowing citizens to “sanction or reward politicians in a periodic manner” (de Vries & Solaz, 2017, p. 391). Although most often associated with national-level politics, elections also take place at the subnational and supranational (Hobolt & de Vries, 2016a) scale, with significant implications for representation and governance.Defining the concept of “elections” becomes less straightforward given that many nondemocratic regimes, both hybrid and fully authoritarian, also organize events labeled as such both by domestic authorities and by external observers, including the media and scholars. Whereas in liberal democracies elections tend to be associated with procedural integrity and meaningful competition, in authoritarian contexts they are often marked by manipulation, including fraud, voter suppression, and the presence of controlled or symbolic opposition (Miller, 2015; Petrov et al., 2014). Moreover, while a strict definition of elections might emphasize the free agency of voter choice, practices such as clientelism and vote buying remain widespread across regimes situated at various points along the democratic–authoritarian continuum (Mares & Young, 2016).This conceptual tension suggests that “elections” can be understood in both narrow and broad senses. In its narrow version, the term refers to the consequential and competitive process of elite selection that defines democratic regimes, serving as a qualitative marker distinguishing democracies from nondemocracies. In the broader sense, it encompasses a wider array of institutionalized procedures—including “non-competitive” but nevertheless substantively relevant elections—that may take place even in the absence of minimally democratic practices (Miller, 2015; Petrov et al., 2014).Elections as a Dependent VariableElections are among the most empirically studied topics in political science, not only due to their centrality in the functioning of political systems but also because they generate a wealth of publicly available data, including electoral records at multiple levels of aggregation. In addition to these official data sources, researchers make substantial efforts to survey citizens, examining whether they voted, how they did so, and why.When studied as a dependent variable, elections have prompted a wide range of research questions and have been empirically operationalized in multiple ways—often through aggregate level data such as turnout rates, party vote shares, indicators of clientelism (Mares & Young, 2016), and institutional constraints (Petrov et al., 2014), but also by using data measured at the individual level, such as voting decisions (Medeiros & Noël, 2014). A central focus has been explaining cross-national and subnational variation in electoral behavior; scholars have devoted much attention to understanding why levels of voter turnout (Cancela & Geys, 2016), support for specific candidates (Scala & Johnson, 2017), and preferences for political platforms (Treib, 2014) vary within and across countries, as well as over time. Researchers have also investigated the impact of electoral rules (Kirkland & Coppock, 2018), campaign dynamics (Fridkin et al., 2015; Jacobson, 2015a), vote-buying attempts (Mares & Young, 2016), and partisanship (Abramowitz & Webster, 2016; Medeiros & Noël, 2014) on voting decisions.Several key patterns emerge from this abundant literature. Electoral systems, campaign mobilization, and levels of political engagement play critical roles in shaping both turnout and the relative strength of candidates and/or parties. Institutional factors such as compulsory voting and the competitiveness of the party system significantly affect participation rates (Cancela & Geys, 2016). Perceptions of corruption also influence turnout and vote choice, though their effects depend on information availability, attribution of blame, and voters’ ability to coordinate an electoral response (de Vries & Solaz, 2017). The erosion of traditional party loyalties has facilitated the rise of new political actors, particularly in contexts marked by regional or national crisis (Turnbull-Dugarte, 2019). Patterns of political competition are also geographically structured, with growing divergence between urban and rural areas shaping both electoral preferences and party strategies (Scala & Johnson, 2017). Overall, scholars in this literature treat elections as encompassing voters’ participation and choices, as well as the dynamics of party competition and alignment.Partisan behavior and patterns of electoral alignment have received increasing attention, especially in the United States (Jacobson, 2015b). There the polarization of the electorate has deepened partisan attachments and fueled the rise of negative partisanship, which has manifested in more consistent party loyalty and a stronger linkage between presidential and lower-level contests, reinforcing the nationalization of electoral behavior (Abramowitz & Webster, 2016). In Europe, disillusionment with mainstream parties has been a key driver of electoral support for populist and Eurosceptic movements, particularly in the wake of the Eurozone crisis (Brack & Startin, 2015; Hobolt & de Vries, 2016a, b; Treib, 2014).Elections as a Driver of Political OutcomesElections are also studied as independent variables, i.e., as factors shaping other political outcomes. The effects of electoral system design on representation and competition are particularly well established. Proportional representation tends to foster multiparty systems, whereas majoritarian systems reinforce two-party dominance. Furthermore, institutional features such as district magnitude, ballot structure, and candidate selection mechanisms shape both voter behavior and legislative outcomes (Kirkland & Coppock, 2018).Beyond shaping competition itself, elections also affect how parties respond to public preferences. Scholars have examined, for instance, how parties and policymakers adjust their strategies and positioning in response to electoral results (Spoon & Klüver, 2014; Treib, 2014), or how reforms to electoral rules influence broader patterns of institutional interaction and legitimacy (Hobolt, 2014). Evidence suggests that party responsiveness varies across electoral contexts, being stronger in national elections and weaker in second-order contests such as European Parliament elections (Spoon & Klüver, 2014).The Role of Elections in Nondemocratic RegimesIn nondemocratic regimes, the function of elections (in the broad sense, as defined above) diverges markedly from their democratic counterparts. Rather than serving as genuine mechanisms for government selection, authoritarian elections often act as instruments of elite coordination, controlled participation, or symbolic legitimation (Miller, 2015). The Russian case illustrates how elections in such settings can be structured to maintain regime stability while offering a façade of democratic procedure (Petrov et al., 2014).Beyond their symbolic and legitimizing function, elections in nondemocratic regimes also serve diagnostic purposes. Regimes use these events to gather information on local grievances, test the loyalty of bureaucratic elites, and calibrate mechanisms of control (Miller, 2015; Petrov et al., 2014). In contexts marked by clientelism or vote buying, such as those analyzed by Mares and Young (2016), elections help reinforce patronage networks and signal access to state resources. Even in the absence of democratic competition, elections (in the broad sense) can play a central role in the reproduction and adaptation of authoritarian rule.Emerging Trends and ChallengesEmerging trends are shaping the future of electoral research. The erosion of democratic norms, the rise of voter suppression tactics, and the strategic manipulation of electoral rules have raised concerns about the legitimacy of elections in both hybrid and formally democratic settings. A key development is the growing influence of digital technologies on electoral dynamics. The spread of political bots and the algorithmic amplification of misinformation pose new challenges to electoral transparency and voter autonomy (Howard et al., 2018). In parallel, the role of emotions and misinformation in shaping voting behavior has gained prominence. Research suggests that negative campaigning and emotionally charged appeals can significantly shape voter perceptions (Medeiros & Noël, 2014), while fact-checking, though limited in reach, plays an important role in countering false or misleading narratives (Fridkin et al., 2015).As electoral contexts continue to evolve, research is increasingly attentive to how institutional design, technological innovation, and voter psychology interact in shaping political behavior. This growing body of work reflects the enduring significance of elections not only as instruments of representation but also as mirrors of broader democratic tensions and transformations.
